#7476. “A government that ‘gets it’”: Canada recommits to federal funding for news

All the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

We have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

The new budget would make a local reporting program permanent and extend a 35% tax credit on newsroom salaries. The support makes “a massive, massive difference.”

A Canadian program to place local reporters in underserved communities has lived from renewal to renewal. Publishers who relied on the Local Journalism Initiative couldn’t be sure whether the money would be there again.

That changed last week when Canada proposed a federal budget that would make the Local Journalism Initiative permanent. The 2026 budget would increase LJI funding to $134 million over four years with $41 million in annual ongoing funding after that. (Figures are, naturally, in Canadian dollars.) For the budget to be finalized, it must pass Parliament. With Prime Minister Mark Carney’s party in the majority, it’s expected to.

Expanding the LJI is not even the biggest piece of federal help for newsrooms, according to Paul Deegan, president and CEO of the news industry advocacy group News Media Canada. The same budget extends a 35% tax credit on newsroom salaries through 2028 and opens it to radio and television newsrooms for the first time. The tax credit will cost $501 million over the next five years, according to the budget. Thanks to the Online News Act, Canadian newsrooms also get funding from Google. And then there’s Canadian investment in public media; the 2026 budget added $300 million over two years to CBC/Radio-Canada “to strengthen its capacity to meet the evolving needs of Canadians across the country.”

I asked Deegan: How did Canadian publishers secure so much federal funding for news?

“We have a government that ‘gets it,’” Deegan said. “They see what Big Tech monopolists have done to local news. They know the labor tax credit is the leading driver of maintaining and growing newsroom headcount.”

RELATED ARTICLECalifornia’s big local news bill becomes lawLaura Hazard OwenOctober 1, 2026There have been similar proposals and experiments in the United States, including a new tax credit in California. But Canada is much further down the road. The country can offer lessons on what it looks like when a federal government commits to supporting journalism.

The labor tax credit refunds 35% of a newsroom employee’s salary, up to $29,750 per journalist per year. The percentage had been scheduled to fall to 25% at the end of 2026.

“In terms of employing the [largest] number of journalists and keeping newsroom employment stability, the labor tax credit is number one,” Deegan said.

There’s also the Online News Act which has brought in $100 million of Google money annually. Of that amount, $63 million is set aside for news publishers. (Meta blocked news on Facebook and Instagram in Canada rather than pay under the Online News Act.) Publishers receive around $17,000 per journalist per year.

“That’s about $47,000 per journalist per year from those two measures,” Deegan said. “That just makes a massive, massive difference.”

In the U.S., some ideas for funding local journalism have been criticized as helping large chain newspapers — including chains that have hollowed out local newsrooms for years. Deegan — whose news industry group counts Postmedia and Torstar as members — acknowledged that the largest share of tax credit dollars goes to the largest employers.

But News Media Canada also represents small and digital-only publications, and Deegan noted the smallest Canadian outlets face another problem. To qualify for the tax credit, an organization must produce original news content and regularly employ at least two journalists “at arm’s length” from its owners. An advisory board found the second rule excludes small “mom-and-pop” newsrooms.

The Local Journalism Initiative is a more targeted program than the tax credit. Launched in 2019, it was designed to support local and community news in underserved areas. The LJI program supports about 470 reporting positions in roughly 1,000 communities across Canada.

Even generous government subsidies have not stopped losses in local news completely. But early results showed the LJI increased reporting capacity and local news in “news poverty” communities with limited local news offerings. The same evaluation identified reaching “news deserts” — communities with no existing local news outlets — and Indigenous communities as obstacles.

“Since LJI is demand driven, funding allocation across the country varies and gaps remain in some areas, such as news deserts,” the report reads. Later, the report notes that allowing news startups “could better support attraction and retainment of journalists” in the neediest communities.

Many of the newsrooms receiving the LJI funding are small. Deegan described family-owned weekly newspapers with circulations as low as 800. Funding provides a local journalist to report on “cops, courts, city hall, and the school board.”

“Without those LJI journalists in some of those communities, those things simply wouldn’t be covered,” he said.

Some underserved communities, particularly in northern Canada, struggle to hire reporters given high living costs and remote locations. “Even with the grant, it’s just hard to recruit and find people,” Deegan noted.

Deegan points to two factors that have made Canada’s federal funding for news work. The first is distance. Publishers get LJI money from one of three administrator organizations: News Media Canada, Community Radio Fund of Canada, or the Consortium of Official Language Minority Community Media. These organizations — not the government itself — administer the funds and an independent board advises on who qualifies for the tax credit.

“To avoid perceptions of conflict of interest, the government ensured that third parties adjudicate who receives local journalism initiative reporters and who is eligible for the labor tax credit,” Deegan said.

The second factor applies to the Online News Act and, more generally, to Canadian politics.

“When it comes to holding those platforms to account, one of the reasons we have been successful is that we have a ban [on] corporate political financing at the federal level in Canada,” Deegan said. “These companies sprinkle goodies around to friendly academics, think tanks, and other useful idiots to do some of their bidding, but our government sees through that nonsense.”

Build programmatic SEO pages that earn their place with unique data, launch checks, and pruning rules that keep scaled publishing from becoming spam.

Generative AI has removed the barrier to publishing at scale. A brand can produce thousands of pages in an afternoon, and even be bold enough to call it programmatic SEO. For many brands, it worked, bringing in massive search traffic and organic revenue.

Management teams also buy in easily, because time to market is short and production costs are low.

Those same two things are now what make it fail. Aggressive programmatic SEO initiatives like these are collapsing or drawing manual penalties, because no one asks whether these pages deserve to exist.

Google has been clear about this. On March 5, 2024, it strengthened its scaled content abuse policy to apply whether automation, humans, or a combination produces the pages, and later reported 45% less low-quality, unoriginal content in results.

On Sept. 7, 2026, John Mueller replied on Bluesky to a site that generated pages from every combination of domain names, technologies, and attributes. He wrote that programmatic SEO of that kind often leads to a site that’s spam, borderline spam, or low quality, and that pages already published may keep shaping how Google judges the whole site.

I have been building programmatic SEO systems since 2016, from static templates to natural language generation engines such as Rosae NLG to AI-assisted pipelines. Some compounded for years and became true case studies for me. Some failed fairly quickly. I have taken that work to conference stages along the way, most recently in a session on scaling pSEO at the Shenzhen SEO Conference.

What we see today is mass AI publishing disguised as programmatic SEO. The real thing starts with a dataset that gives every page something a visitor can use. This article draws the line between the two.

Programmatic SEO is a way of publishing, not a kind of content. It has three parts: a repeatable search pattern, a structured dataset that makes each page unique and value-driven, and a template that answers the query for every variation.

Take a currency converter. The pattern is “convert X to Y,” the dataset is a live rate for every currency pair, and the template turns each row into a page. Nobody writes thousands of pages by hand. The data makes each page different. And you publish only as many pages as your data can support.

Lucia Lecesne, the Marketing Lead of Wise, which runs exactly that kind of program, says:

“At Wise, we focus on genuine customer utility: solving a problem that users face on their journey to become customers. Programmatic SEO can then make that solution relevant and accessible across the many search queries and modifiers that share the same problem, in other words, tailoring it to each customer’s specific search context. It should never be a shortcut to publishing large volumes of low-quality pages.”

Mass AI publishing looks the same from the outside, which is why the two get confused. It keeps the template and the publishing system, but what makes each page different comes from a prompt. Swap the city name, and you have a new page with nothing new on it.

Google’s policies draw the same line. The word “programmatic” does not appear in its spam policies. What does appear is scaled content abuse: many pages generated mainly to manipulate rankings rather than help users, no matter how it’s created. Using generative AI to generate many pages without adding value is one of its named examples.

A template isn’t what gets penalized, and neither is automation. The core question worth evaluating is whether each page adds value.

Here is a quick test. Picture two pages for “cost of living in Lisbon,” built from the same template and the same search pattern. The first shows rent ranges, transport passes, and grocery prices pulled from a maintained dataset, and it updates when the numbers change.

The second looks just as complete, with a rent figure, a monthly budget, and a confident summary, but the numbers are the model’s best guess. They carry no source and no date, and the same sentences appear on every other city page with only the name changed. Only the first is programmatic SEO. To tell them apart, ask where each number on the page came from and when it was last updated. The first page can answer. The second can’t.

See also: How Do You Fix Thin Content Across Similar Ecommerce Product Pages? – Ask An SEO

Most teams can’t say whether their pages are programmatic SEO or mass publishing, because the output looks the same from the outside. These six checks look underneath it.

None of these checks ask whether AI wrote the page. A page built on real data and drafted with AI can still perform well, while a hand-written page with no real data behind it has no more claim to rank. Treat the comparison rubric as a diagnostic: if one of the rows fails, you have a workflow problem to fix. If several parameters fail, then you are mass publishing, whatever you call it.

Eli Schwartz draws the line in the same place, and argues:

“Spinning up pages just because you can isn’t SEO; it’s programmatic spam. If you create pages because they benefit many users, that is good SEO, whether you create them programmatically or manually.”

Danny Sullivan, then Google’s Search Liaison, shared a way to test this at a 2025 event. The question, in his words as Search Engine Journal reported, is whether the intent was “‘I’m going to get that traffic’ and not ‘some user actually expected it'” if they came to your site directly. Ask that of your own pages: would a visitor who arrived straight at your site ever land on this one on purpose?

The pages I built in 2016 and the ones I build today look very similar. Shipping a bad one is the part that got easy. I walked through that early scaling playbook at BrightonSEO in 2022.

The middle era is the one I think about most. A rule-based engine like Rosae NLG writes sentences from structured data, and it only says what the data and the template author allow. It was slow to build, and that slowness was doing useful work.

Language models took that limit away. A model will write a fluent, confident paragraph about a row with nothing in it, and a reader cannot tell. I covered where AI belongs in a pSEO pipeline, and where it does not, at ISS Barcelona in 2024.

So the checks evolved. People do the research and decide each page’s structure, the model drafts the sections from that structure, and a subject matter expert reviews the facts and brand fit before anything goes live.

Language models did not make programmatic SEO better or worse. We used to be stopped by the tools. Now we have to stop ourselves, and the checklist below is how I do it.

In my experience, the programs that have survived and thrived across multiple Google updates had a written rule for deleting pages before they needed one.

That is close to how Kevin Indig describes the failure mode in a direct message with me:

“Programmatic SEO usually goes wrong when it is ‘spray and pray: publishing a lot of pages at once with no experimentation, no refreshing, and no look at engagement.’ The fix is the one worth underlining: treat pSEO like its own product, not like a content batch.”

Search is changing underneath these programs. In the first four months of 2026, 68% of U.S. Google searches ended without a click, according to SparkToro’s analysis of Similarweb data. That’s up from about 60% in 2024 and about 45% in 2016. SparkToro points to AI Overviews, which it says now appear on more than 20% of searches, and Ahrefs estimates they cut clicks on the top result by 58%.

For a programmatic page, that changes the goal. Traffic can’t be the only test of whether a page earns its place, because the click may never come. What stays is influence: Rand Fishkin notes that your content still shapes AI answers and Google’s other zero-click features even as visits fall.

“pSEO doesn’t fail because it’s programmatic; it fails when scale replaces substance. The hard part isn’t the tech; it’s the discipline to never trade quality for volume, because pSEO makes that trade tempting for every decision maker.

The test hasn’t changed. If a page’s only value was that it ranked, zero-click search takes away its reason to exist. If the value was the data, an AI answer still has to point to it. Before you scale anything, pick one page and ask where each number on it came from.

ONA, OpenNews, and others see troubled times ahead, so it’s goodbye to “rubber chicken dinners.”

RELATED ARTICLEWe know coronavirus has wrecked the events business for media in 2020. But will it come back post-virus?Joshua BentonMarch 25, 2020When the pandemic forced conferences to go virtual, the question was whether people would come back in person post-Covid.

For a while, they did. For a couple years after the pandemic, people were excited to be in person together again. U.S. journalism organizations saw their revenue climb, as sponsors and funders spent generously.

At the end of 2026, though, the situation is less rosy. Combine surging jet fuel prices, inflation, media companies cutting costs, and declining sponsor and funder dollars, and the future appears grim not just for journalism conferences but, in some cases, for the organizations behind them.

Revenue is the total revenue line on each organization’s IRS Form 990. The 990s are from ProPublica’s Nonprofit Explorer. ONA’s 990 for 2025 was not available as of November 12, 2026.

The Online News Association said on Tuesday that it is “pausing” its 26-year-old conference and laying off its five staffers.

“Before the pandemic, the annual conference was ONA’s biggest source of revenue, and together with grants, it sustained the organization. This is no longer true,” Niketa Patel wrote. “The costs of large convenings have climbed sharply while professional development and sponsorship budgets have shrunk.”

LION Publishers said in September that it’s getting out of the large conference business for now. “Philanthropy is famously fickle, and funding priorities have shifted, making this kind of conference a very tough lift,” executive director Chris Krewson added.

LION barely broke even on the conferences it held in 2025 and 2026, Krewson told me. The organization may still hold smaller events next year, it’s not cutting staff or programming, and it’s expanding its Audit program. But it “won’t be taking on the responsibility for an independent event at a hotel with a food and beverage minimum and hotel room block for 400-plus people.”

“Every dollar I spend on rubber chicken dinners and microphones/WiFi for three days is money I can’t spend on programs that make publishers’ businesses stronger,” Krewson said.

OpenNews said in October that it’s switching into “emergency mode”1 and cutting back on “work that distills journalism craft: no more community calls or Source articles for at least the rest of 2026 and maybe longer.”

The future of OpenNews’s annual conference, SRCCON, is uncertain. “We usually make our decision about SRCCON at about this time every year, but this year is different as we consider the news from both LION and ONA and the funding pressures that we know all too well,” Jessica Morrison, co–executive director of OpenNews, told me in an email. “We are opening a community conversation today — emails going out very soon — to gather input about SRCCON, our other programs, and where we go next with OpenNews.”

The three-year-old Organization for Accessible Journalism said Thursday that it is shutting down. “Financial support never reached a level that allowed us to build beyond an all volunteer effort — including my full-time effort,” founder Stacy Kess wrote.

Journalism conferences in the United States are certainly not gone. IRE and NICAR will hold their annual data journalism conference in Denver in March. The Institute for Nonprofit News is “talking about what INN Days will look like in 2027” and will know more by early next year. And the International Symposium on Journalism is on for 2027 — its 28th year, founder (and Nieman Foundation board member) Rosental Alves told me. But things have gotten harder, he said. “It’s not only the difficulty of finding sponsors, but also the rising costs of venues, hotels, airfares, etc., compounded by shrinking travel budgets in newsrooms and even the problems international attendees face in coming to the U.S.,” he told me in an email. ISOJ cut costs, in part by moving to a different venue, and it benefits from being relatively small. “It’s very sad that foundations and corporations that funded journalism conferences in the past have pulled back their support,” Alves added. “The need for these gatherings is as great as ever.” a play on Emergency Mode for News, its initiative to support journalists working during disasters [↩]

#7470. Google Releases Modern Web Guidance 1.0 For AI Coding Agents via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Spend less time on publishing and reports, and more on helpful content. November 18, 2 PM ET.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Webinar: 9 AI Workflows For Better Content. Nov 18, 2 PM ET.

A free skill set for AI coding agents leaves preview with a codebase audit and public evals. One early test scored higher when agents were told to use it.

Google issued version 1.0 of Modern Web Guidance, which is a free skill set that web development teams may use as an enhancement to their AI coding tools, in order for those tools to write code based on current browser features. The skills are in the form of packaged guidelines that the agent will look at while writing the code. The code generated by the agent will also be sent to the same pages that are evaluated for metrics such as Largest Contentful Paint (LCP), Interaction to Next Paint (INP), and accessibility.

Philip Walton, a senior staff developer relations engineer at Google, announced the release in a Chrome for Developers post. Version 1.0 adds an audit for existing code, and Firefox and Edge are joining the project. Chrome first released the guidance as an early preview at Google I/O in May.

Teams can install it by running npx modern-web-guidance@latest install in a project directory. It’s also available through the plugin marketplaces of most popular coding agents, according to the post.

Version 1.0’s audit will go through a project’s HTML, CSS, JavaScript files as well as its package.json to identify areas where developers are able to safely update their code, then walk the agent through the changes. This first iteration of the audit uses static analysis to look at a limited number of code patterns, according to the post.

The post says the library now targets “hundreds of verified AI knowledge gaps” across its guides. Additionally, current coding models continue to fall short in Google’s tests of accessibility, security headers, and loading priority for scripts and images.

According to Google, each of the guides is now reviewed and approved by a domain tech lead. For user-facing feature guides there is a dedicated accessibility review done by experts who use assistive technologies daily.

A governance document was uploaded to the project’s GitHub repository on Nov. 9 which outlines six owner seats for the project. Two of those seats belong to Chrome, Microsoft Edge and Mozilla each have one, and two are given to independent web platform experts. There is currently one open independent seat and no seat belongs to Apple.

Google’s announcement links to a public eval dashboard where coding agents from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google run the same set of tasks every night, with and without the guidance. A real browser then checks the DOM, styles and source code of each finished app.

When I checked Tuesday morning, guided runs were passing 88% of the automated checks, whereas unguided runs were passing 56%. These figures are based upon each agent’s combined results for nightly runs completed Nov. 8; the range is 199 to 215 tasks per agent. The dashboard provides a limited review (not a full WCAG audit, it says) of accessibility features such as support for keyboards, focus, and form labels.

Its task prompts don’t mention the guidance, so each agent has to work out on its own when a guide applies. In most of the recent suites listed, guided runs ran slower and burned more tokens.

Accessibility consultant Adrian Roselli evaluated the preview in May by giving Antigravity (Google’s AI coding tool) an animated accordion prompt found in the documentation. However, according to Roselli, the output did not comply with WCAG and its animation was not functional in Firefox. He also found no assurance that agents would be able to follow the guidelines. This was for the preview, not v1.0.

The new guidelines were tested by Japan’s creator platform, note inc. using two coding agents that ran through six user interface (UI) tasks across 180 test runs on clone versions of note inc.’s production code base. As explained in a Chrome blog, both agents’ scores on 19 browser checks rose after installing the skill without naming it in prompts, then again once prompts named it. Agent One went from 60.8% to 76.5% to 94.0%. Similarly, Agent Two had scores of 75.8%, 86.2%, and 90.0% under the same three test conditions.

One of note’s tasks checked whether the largest image in view on an article page had high priority and wasn’t lazy-loaded. The comparison table in the post shows that unguided agents wrote hero image code using both high priority and lazy loading.

The guidance is run by MetaMask, as part of an automatic review process for each pull request submitted to its open-source browser extension, according to a second Chrome post. Through Oct. 21 (the first five weeks), the bot identified 102 issues across 57 feature and fix pull requests. The engineers fully resolved 43 of them and partially resolved three of them. Another 16 were either declined or false positives. Twenty of them went unaddressed. The outcome of the other 20 is unknown.

Modern Web Guidance provides a no-cost means for teams to encourage agents writing code to use native browser capabilities and that includes code in existing legacy code bases. Most of the results that have been published are based on testing conducted by Google as well as customer testing that Google highlighted. Note Inc. tested the two agents using the same prompt with and without telling them to use the guidance; they both performed better when the prompt did tell them to use the guidance. The team can also label their prompts to include the guidance and keep field data and manual accessibility testing in the review.

Google says it plans to expand this process of auditing existing code at some point, as well as performing audits in which the agent is reasoning about the actual code being audited.

The company suggests pairing the guidance with Chrome DevTools for agents to allow the agent to run its own created code and test it inside of the browser. Preview users can use the command npx modern-web-guidance@latest update.

On Wednesday, Meta, TikTok, and Google testified in the Indonesian parliament in opposition to a new copyright bill. The proposed law would require digital platforms to pay news publishers in Indonesia for aggregating and previewing their content, according to a new report from Reuters.

RELATED ARTICLEThis citizen-run organization is teaching thousands of Indonesians to fact-checkHanaa' TameezApril 12, 2023The bill does not distinguish between aggregation and republication. Tech platforms would have to pay even when they surface news link previews or story snippets in their products, including AI search products. The law would also force platforms to compensate publishers when their journalism is used to train AI models.

Any compensation would be paid through a state-run management organization, which would then distribute the funds to publishers. Platforms that don’t comply could face sanctions, including the loss of their local business permits.

If the bill does pass, Indonesia would become the first country in Southeast Asia to formally fold AI into its copyright law.

Social media and search engine companies have come out in force against the bill, with Google leading the campaign.

Indonesia is a massive market for global digital platforms with roughly 230 million internet users. In 2023, Indonesia had the fifth-most Google users of any country in the world, with traffic reaching 4.42 billion searches.

RELATED ARTICLEMeta will remove legit news from Facebook and Instagram in Canada — but may leave the bad stuff upLaura Hazard OwenAugust 2, 2023As of October 2026, 92% of internet users in Indonesia reported using WhatsApp, with Instagram and Facebook falling close behind at 84% and 79% respectively, according to We Are Social’s Digital 2027 report.

On Wednesday, a Google official argued that the bill would limit access to news, according to Reuters.

Berni Moestafa, Meta’s head of public policy in Indonesia, testified that if the bill is passed “publishers could lose readership traffic as well as potential advertising and subscription revenue.”

Back in 2023, Canada passed the Online News Act, its own, albeit narrower law which required platforms like Google and Meta to pay publishers for sharing or linking to their content. Meta responded by blocking news links on Facebook and Instagram in Canada altogether.

#7466. “F*** Keywords” – Well, What Are You Replacing Them With? via @sejournal, @chrisgreenseo

Identify practical ways to improve location visibility in AI-generated answers and recommendations.

This rundown shows how to test briefs, audits, or rank reporting with a four-layer system built on your own data.

Spend less time on publishing and reports, and more on helpful content. November 18, 2 PM ET.

Invalid traffic on AI Max search doubled to 5.28%. Get the channel-by-channel retail benchmarks before Black Friday.

Ask the SEJ experts you already read what AI, agents, and algorithm changes mean for your traffic. Private, human to human. $97/mo.

Declaring keywords dead is easy. Explaining what you’ll track, how you’ll govern content, and what stakeholders buy into is the harder part.

Every so often, someone in SEO announces “f*** keywords” or a similar sentiment. It’s not really a “hot take.” Moreover, it’s something that we see time and again.

Sometimes it’s a fair reaction to how reluctant some people in the industry are to change. Other times it feels more like a meme response, or a flex. A way to show you’ve moved on from old-school SEO without saying much about what you do differently, exaggerating a tension between pro/anti keywords without understanding it.

I have some sympathy for the sentiment for sure. I’ve worked on too many campaigns where success came down to whether a handful of keywords went up or down. Once those rankings became THE GOAL, it was easy to spend more time explaining two dropped places than asking whether we met the primary business need. More damagingly, in the worst cases we were left making decisions just for promoting keywords, rather than the business goals they were supposed to enable.

I don’t know how many people still run campaigns that way, and I suspect fewer than the “f*** keywords” cry implies. What interests me is how quickly the argument goes from “this is a bad way to judge a campaign” to “why are we thinking about keywords at all?”

Take an example search like [hotels near Heathrow with a shuttle]. It’s a decent shorthand for what someone wants to know before they book. Is there a shuttle to the terminal? Does it run when my flight lands? Do I need to reserve a seat? It also gives you a clue about what language you need to use to gain recognition from the searcher.

If guests are looking for a shuttle, the page titled “ground transportation solutions” is making them do more work than they need to. Again, a fictitious example, but I have lost track of how many times in my career I’ve seen businesses wanting to target the ways they define their products/services, NOT how people search for them.

In this instance, what is more important is that the initial search query becomes emblematic of a series of questions that need answering, potentially across a series of pages. Whether we call this a hub and spoke model, or a content cluster, whatever, we have captured part of the customer journey with a query and then determined the potential related queries.

This is where a keyword map (or site map) earns its keep, long after the initial research is done and the content written and published. Imagine that six months later someone rewrites a particular location page. The shuttle timetable moves into a general FAQ and a new transfers page goes live. All three changes are totally logical, but taken together, they can leave the site without a clear place to answer the question the location page used to own. Without realizing it, you have sleepwalked into undoing the research you have done before.

If you’ve recorded which page serves that need, the next content editor or SEO has something to go back to. They can ensure that intent/search query is still considered, move content responsibility, update the internal links, and ensure the redirects are done. The keyword map preserves the reasoning behind those original decisions and helps you tell the difference between an intentional change and targeting that drifted over a few rounds of perfectly reasonable edits.

The keywords aren’t the single truth, nor are they to be treated as an immutable dogma, but throwing them in the “f***it bucket” could be missing something important.

Too cool for keywords now? Great, but how does governance work? How do you ensure you’re not wasting the money already spent on research? Yeah, I know – that sounds tedious, because it can be. And building a process to make sure this isn’t painfully manual IS hard.

You can organize your work around topics, and you can use embeddings to help group the language – in fact you should! But at some point, you’ll at least need to benchmark overall visibility, and you still have to choose what to type into a search box or put in a prompt. You can aggregate your rank/prompt tracking for a content cluster – which is needed – but before the aggregation comes selections of individual prompts and terms.

Stakeholders need to buy into those prompts/terms/queries that make up that group OR you 10x the number of specific tracked elements to totally de-emphasize any individual one. Not a bad idea, but you increase your costs significantly and still need to consider the wording, terms and intents on individual pages when it comes to making optimizations.

Instead, I’d happily track a few representative searches for a given page, where I would also want to see which URL(s) appeared and whether they answered the question. Those observations can tell us whether the page is doing some of the work we intended, whether another page is potentially conflicting and where our own content is falling behind competitors.

“Wait, we still use keywords in our data, but we don’t report on the success of individual keywords anymore!” That is perfectly sensible, but it turns out that maybe, perhaps, the “f*** keywords” position is more clickbait than actual smart thinking – right?

These are SEO basics; I totally understand. Prompt tracking and AI search do ultimately de-emphasize the importance of exact keywords in favor of meaning. But consider that embedding text into vectors is so “machines” can understand it. Your team, colleagues and stakeholders still need the human version to understand how to optimize and tell the story of what is/isn’t working.

All of this helps us understand what we’re visible for, but it doesn’t tell us what happened next – and that is perhaps the biggest weakness.

In Search City, I wrote about the temptation to only optimize for the bits of the search journey we can see. Rankings were always one of the easier bits to observe – that is why we have had an almighty job replacing them with a more useful metric, and why the issues hitting prompt trackers are so disruptive to the industry! But now, even when someone makes a search and sees you for that query/keyword/prompt, the part that links that moment to a click and then an important business event can be almost totally disconnected.

Knowing whether we “rank” for a keyword or not is still an important data point. Fixating on that single data point is mad – but that goes for any single data point. We need to use it to build the picture, build a story and provide insight.

If I went back to any of those campaigns I ran where I felt single terms were prioritized (to a fault), I’d probably still keep some of the same keywords – as triggering as that may be.

I’d use them to agree which searches mattered the most, decide which pages should serve them and check whether those pages still do the job. When it came time to judge the campaign, I’d want to know what happened to the customers/clicks we were trying to win. That was the question the rankings were supposed to help us answer in the first place, and it is still something they can help answer today.

This post was originally published on Chris Green SEO.

Google is expanding ads in AI Mode to 10+ countries in English and launching multiturn ads in the U.S. Here is what PPC advertisers need to know about reporting.

Google is expanding ads in AI Mode to more than 10 new countries in English while launching multiturn ads for follow-up queries in the U.S.

Google shared the update from its official Google Ads X account on November 9, following an earlier LinkedIn post from Dan Taylor noting plans to bring ads in AI Mode to additional countries in Q4.

Eligible campaigns can already participate, though advertisers still can’t see AI Mode performance separately in Google Ads.

Here’s what’s changing, how conversational placements work, and what you need to know when clients ask about AI Mode reporting.

Google’s October announcement named 10 additional countries where ads in AI Mode are expanding:

The expansion currently supports English. Google also announced plans to bring ads in AI Mode to Brazil, Mexico, and the United Kingdom in Q4 2026. Those markets were listed as upcoming rather than part of the initial rollout.

Google’s availability documentation notes that Pakistan supports text ads only.

Multiturn ads are launching in the U.S., allowing ads to appear on follow-up questions within an AI Mode conversation. Google hasn’t announced when those placements will expand outside the U.S.

Google describes AI Mode as a search experience for questions involving exploration, reasoning, or complex comparisons. Users can ask a detailed question an dcontinue with follow-ups as they work through their options.

AI Mode may use “query fan-out,” issuing related searches across subtopics and data sources to develop a response.

With multiturn ads, Google can show an ad during those follow-up exchanges when the conversation has commercial relevance.

According to Google’s advertiser documentation, ads can match directly to a search query or draw on context from both the question and AI response. An exploratory question can then create an advertising opportunity even when the user hasn’t searched for a specific product.

In his LinkedIn update, Taylor noted that people are asking longer, more detailed, and exploratory questions in AI Mode, and described many of those interactions as upper-funnel queries that carry commercial intent.

For advertisers, that means ads may reach people still comparing approaches or deciding what they need. A longer question or another follow-up does not, on its own, indicate that someone is ready to buy.

As ads in AI Mode expand, clients will likely ask whether their campaigns are appearing there and how those ads perform.

In my view, the most important thing for agency and in-house teams to communicate right now is that reporting is limited, and you can’t separate out AI Mode performance granularly.

Google’s reporting documentation confirms that AI Mode impressions, clicks, conversions, and costs are included in standard campaign reporting. Search terms are also combined with other traffic, without a separate AI Mode breakdown. That prevents advertisers from calculating an AI Mode-specific CPA or ROAS.

Google’s keyword prioritization documentation also says reported search terms for experiences including AI Mode may approximate the user’s intent. Advertisers should not assume they are seeing the exact question someone entered.

Teams can still review those terms for relevance, compare conversion performance, and check lead quality. If results change after the rollout, though, the timing alone can’t directly establish that AI Mode caused it.

When clients ask how AI Mode ads are performing, advertisers can explain that those results are included in campaign totals. Google Ads doesn’t report them separately, so teams can’t show how much spend or how many conversions came from AI Mode.

Google is adding countries and follow-up placements without giving advertisers a separate view of their results.

That leaves teams answering questions about AI Mode with campaign-level data. A campaign could improve overall while AI Mode underperforms, or the reverse, and the combined totals wouldn’t show that granularity.

Separate reporting would help advertisers understand which searches and placements are producing sales or qualified leads. Until Google provides it, teams can explain how their campaigns qualify for AI Mode, but can’t necessarily tell clients what those placements contributed to.

#7462. Why Rao’s heated up brand building with a request to slow down meals

The Campbell Company sauce brand reimagines the concept of a limited-time offer by keying in on how many meals people have left with loved ones.

Rao’s Homemade today revealed a four-minute short film that reimagines the concept of a limited-time offer by reminding consumers that the most limited time is the time people spend together, per details shared with Marketing Dive. “Limited-Time Only” was directed by Aqsa Altaf and John X. Carey, the duo known as Aqsa + John X. who were behind Dove’s “Real Beauty Sketches” campaign.

“Limited-Time Only” shares the story of three individuals as they are interviewed about how often they have dinner with family. The heart-tugging video culminates with each being presented a jar of Rao’s sauce labeled with an estimate of how many meals they have left with certain family members before being surprised with a dinner with their loved ones.

The short film is part of a larger “Make Time” campaign created with Goodby Silverstein & Partners that spans premium video, social, influencer, public relations, retail media and owned channels.

In a survey of more than 1,000 individuals and in-depth interviews with 200 people, the brand and agency learned that 84% of Americans wish they shared more meals with loved ones, yet only one-third of families actually sit down together. The campaign unites those findings with product truths about the time-intensive way Rao’s sauce is made, from hand-picked tomatoes and hand-peeled onions and garlic that are simmered for hours.

“It's not just about the food; It's about the experience that creating that food enables, and it's an opportunity to really slow down and savor the food and to savor those that you're sitting around the table with, and to make meal time less of a transaction and more of an experience and an opportunity to connect with others,” said Chris Tutor, vice president of advertising and design at Rao’s parent The Campbell Company.

That experience was captured in a series of ads that feature groups of people enjoying a meal and include taglines like “the best part of the day is sharing it” and “keep long stories long.” The spots are set to live orchestral music and end with a scarpetta, the Italian tradition of using bread to mop up the last of the sauce. The creation of those spots led the team to investigate the larger narrative around meals with loved ones that informed “Limited-Time Only.”

“The long-form [video] allowed us to tell more of that story from the impetus for it to the aha moment to then the celebratory moment, and it really allowed us to blow out that visceral moment around the table into the full story,” Tutor said.

While “Limited-Time Only” does not have a traditional ad length, the creative is in line with a trend around longer-form content that marketers have adopted to tell more engaging stories to consumers. Depending on the platform, the brand will either run the long-form asset or teasers that point to the full video.

“There's been a lot of media attention around this idea, and so we’re leveraging media partners to help tell the story,” Tutor said. “Setting up the context before watching the film will also, we think, drive a lot of eyeballs to it. We're trying to do the math and science of making sure the right piece of content shows up on the right channel at the right time.”

The Campbell Company acquired Rao’s parent Sovos Brands for $2.7 billion deal in March 2024. Rao’s is a billion-dollar brand for Campbell’s and continues to grow, with consumption up 11.3% in fiscal year 2026. To fuel this growth, Rao’s increased media spending and will further increase it in fiscal 2027, executives said on a recent earnings call.

While Rao’s has grown household penetration, it still lags behind sister brand Prego. The “Make Time” campaign is key to the brand’s marketing efforts and represents both a brand building story and an awareness play.

“As people become aware of the brand or if they're already aware of the brand, what does the brand stand for beyond just that exceptional food? It's bringing this notion of slow living to every meal, reminding people that life tastes better when it's savored, and establishing what the brand means on an emotional level, versus just a rational level,” Tutor said.

Google's latest core update is rolling out worldwide in all languages. The company calls it a regular update, and rankings may move during the rollout.

Google began rolling out the November 2026 core update today, according to the Google Search Status Dashboard. The rollout started at 10:06 a.m. PT. Google says the update applies globally and to all languages and may take up to two weeks to complete.

The company’s Search Central account also announced the update on LinkedIn. It’s the third Search core update this year. Google recommends waiting until the rollout is complete before checking your Search Console data.

Google’s Search Status Dashboard entry reads:

“Released the November 2026 core update, which applies globally and to all languages. The rollout may take up to 2 weeks to complete.”

“This is a regular update designed to better surface relevant, satisfying content for searchers from all types of sites.”

The exact wording in that sentence is what Google used for its March core update.

As of posting time, no specific objectives are mentioned on either the dashboard entry or the LinkedIn post. The Search Central blog doesn’t have a post regarding the update either. Google’s core updates page carries a revision date of Dec. 10, 2025.

The May core update finished rolling out on June 2, more than five months before today’s launch. Three spam updates ran in between.

The November update is the eighth ranking update listed on the Search Status Dashboard so far this year.

Some sites may experience rank changes during the rollout of the November core update. Google’s core updates document advises waiting at least a full week after the completion of a core update, then comparing your Search Console data from that week to a week prior to the start of the rollout. Google’s suggested baseline in advance of the November update is a week prior to Nov. 10.

A full two-week rollout would finish around Nov. 24. The week immediately following Nov. 24 will include U.S. Thanksgiving, Black Friday and Cyber Monday. Retail sites looking at this time period compared to a pre-update week would be looking at holiday traffic against a regular week.

According to Google, core updates don’t target specific sites or individual pages and are meant to keep its systems current as content on the web changes.

Per its LinkedIn post, Google will update its ranking release history page once the rollout is complete. We’ll update this article then, too.
